q: During a large emergency rescue, when must a unique identifier and individual record be formally established for each incoming animal?
o: Within 72 hours of entering the adoption gallery
At or prior to admission, ensuring consistency and accuracy in care and record-keeping from the start
Only after the animal has been scanned for a microchip three separate times
After the first scheduled population round
e: The ASV mandate is clear: unique ID and individual record must be established at or prior to admission. Any care provided before this point cannot be reliably attributed to the correct animal, creating both clinical and legal risk.

q: Which list correctly identifies all nine mandatory fundamental intake information items required for an individual record?
o: Unique ID, intake type, intake date, species, age/category, sex, spay-neuter status, physical description, and weight or BCS
Microchip brand, behavior score, adult weight, rabies tag color, crate location, donor name, and diet type
Breed purity percentage, zip code, surrender fee status, coat length, and adopter restrictions
Pathogen exposure risk index, target length of stay, and slow-track pathway number
e: All nine Phase A items are: unique identifier, intake type, intake date, species, age or age category, sex, spay-neuter status, physical description, and weight or BCS. Any other combination is incomplete.

q: An intake technician is reviewing a dog's record for the identification triad. Which three assets must be present to meet the mandatory identification standard?
o: Owner's driver's license copy, a rabies certificate, and pedigree papers
A photograph of the animal, microchip scan results, and specific identifying markings
Weight chart, body condition score, and a dental aging chart
Map of the intake location, cage card color, and behavioral profile score
e: The identification triad consists of: (1) a photograph of the animal taken at intake, (2) microchip scan results (positive with chip number, or negative), and (3) identifying markings. Together, these legally bind the physical animal to its digital record.

q: An owned cat is being surrendered due to a housing change. Which element of the cat's vaccination history must be explicitly sought and documented?
o: The manufacturer name of the first feline herpesvirus vaccine
The rabies vaccination history
The exact time the last feline panleukopenia booster was administered
A signed affidavit confirming no bordetella exposure
e: The ASV framework specifically names rabies vaccination history as a mandatory history item. This is because rabies status directly drives quarantine decisions and legal obligations in bite cases. General vaccine history is required, but rabies is the one explicitly called out by name.

q: A shelter encounters a canine influenza outbreak. The epidemiological team needs to identify which animals shared airspace with the index case over the past 14 days. Which tracking parameter provides this data?
o: The nine fundamental intake information items
Housing locations by time recorded under in-shelter care activities
The unique identification number and name
The animal's historical home environment details
e: Housing locations logged by time is the only record parameter that allows the team to reconstruct which animals occupied the same area as the index case during the relevant incubation window. This is why real-time housing tracking is mandated, not just a best practice.

q: An animal is being transferred to an outside rescue organization. Which two data points must be added to the record to officially document this outcome?
o: The recipient organization's annual budget and the transport vehicle's license plate
Outcome type (Transfer to Rescue) and the exact date of the outcome
Total weight change during the stay and the final behavioral assessment grade
Name of the transfer coordinator and total days in foster care
e: Every shelter stay must conclude with two mandatory outcome fields: the outcome type (in this case, Transfer to Rescue) and the exact date of the outcome. Both must be recorded to close the file and enable accurate live release rate and ALOS calculations.

q: A shelter supervisor audits the database and finds five kittens housed together under one collective file labeled 'Litter 404B' with no individual records. What rule does this violate?
o: Litters must only be tracked individually if assigned to a slow-track behavioral pathway
Every animal must have a unique identification number and an individual record, regardless of housing arrangement
Group files are permitted if all animals in the group share an identical physical description
Individual records are required only for animals older than 5 months of age
e: The fundamental mandate requires one unique ID and one individual record per animal, with no exceptions. Group housing does not permit group records. Each of the five kittens requires a separate file from the point of admission.

q: An intake clerk logs a dog as 'Stray, found at 5th and Main Street.' Which of the nine fundamental intake items does the word 'Stray' fulfill?
o: Unique identifier
Physical description
Intake type
Age category
e: 'Stray' identifies the intake type, one of the nine mandatory Phase A items. It distinguishes this animal from owner surrenders, transfers, OIE admissions, returns, and animals born in care, which have different holding period and outcome implications.

q: An intake technician photographs a dog's unique facial scars and cropped ears at admission. Under which record category do these images fall?
o: Historical home environment details
In-shelter behavioral findings
Photograph of the animal and identifying markings (the ID triad)
Outcome type metadata
e: Intake photographs and documentation of specific physical markings are components of the identification triad (Phase B). They legally bind the physical animal to the digital record. Behavioral findings are a separate in-shelter care activity category.

q: A shelter manager wants to analyze the relationship between an animal's physical condition at intake and its ultimate length of stay. Which specific Phase A item must be reviewed?
o: Medical treatments and procedures received in shelter care
Weight or Body Condition Score (BCS)
The precise date of the outcome
Historical data on people and animals lived with
e: Weight or Body Condition Score (BCS) is the Phase A item that captures physical condition status at intake. It is the ninth of the nine mandatory fundamental intake items and is the one most commonly omitted in non-compliant records.

q: A surrendered cat's history notes that she hid under furniture during thunderstorms and lived with two young children. Under which history category do these details belong?
o: Fundamental intake physical description
Behavioral events and experiences, people and animals lived with, and home environment
In-shelter care housing locations by time
Microchip scan results and unique identifier fields
e: Hiding behavior (behavioral event), child household members (people lived with), and noise sensitivity (home environment) all fall under Phase C historical context. These three of the five history sub-items capture the animal's pre-shelter life experiences.

q: A technician administers core vaccines and an anthelmintic to a puppy in the intake room. Where in the individual record must these clinical actions be documented?
o: Vaccination history from the previous owner (Phase C history)
In-shelter care activities: medical findings, treatments, and procedures
Fundamental intake type and date metadata (Phase A)
Phase C historical context data fields
e: Any clinical action performed by shelter staff during the animal's stay is documented under in-shelter care activities, specifically under medical findings, treatments, and procedures. Owner-provided vaccination history is a different and separate Phase C field.

q: A dog develops barrier frustration in Run 12 and is moved to a behavioral rehab ward. The behavior team modifies its daily management plan. Which combination of record fields must be updated?
o: Primary unique identifier and intake type
Behavioral findings, plans, and treatments, plus housing locations by time
Rabies vaccination history and physical description
Microchip scan brand and final outcome date
e: Two in-shelter tracking fields require updating: (1) behavioral findings and updated management plan under behavioral findings and plans, and (2) the housing location record showing the move from Run 12 to the rehab ward with the date of transfer.

q: A senior cat passes away naturally overnight in her enclosure. The care team records 'Died in Kennel' in her file. This entry satisfies which mandatory record category?
o: In-shelter medical procedure log
Phase A fundamental physical description
Outcome type
Behavioral history event log
e: 'Died in Kennel' is the outcome type. Natural death, euthanasia, adoption, transfer, and RTO are all documented as outcome types paired with the exact date of the outcome to close the record.

q: A volunteer asks why two dogs of the same breed and color cannot share an ID number. What is the core reason for requiring a unique ID for each animal?
o: To enable the shelter to charge higher adoption fees for rare physical descriptions
To ensure consistency and accuracy in care and record-keeping for each specific individual
To automatically calculate the shelter's total staffing capacity hours
To eliminate the need for intake photographs
e: Unique IDs are mandated to guarantee that every piece of clinical, behavioral, and logistical information is reliably attributed to the correct individual animal. Shared IDs corrupt medical records, outbreak investigations, and outcome statistics.

q: An inspector finds a dog's file with a name, intake date, species, age, physical description, and weight recorded, but no documentation of sex or spay-neuter status. What type of compliance failure has occurred?
o: Sex and spay-neuter status are among the nine mandatory Phase A items; their absence is a record compliance failure
Missing sex data automatically invalidates the microchip scan results
Spay-neuter status is only required for slow-track behavioral candidates
The inspector cannot calculate required holding capacity without this information
e: Sex and spay-neuter status are items 6 and 7 of the nine mandatory Phase A items. Their omission from the record is a direct compliance failure under the ASV record-keeping standard, regardless of any other information present.

q: A stray dog arrives with completely unknown background. What is the correct approach to the vaccination history field in its individual record?
o: Invent a placeholder rabies vaccination date to satisfy the software
Document that history is unknown for each applicable field, maintaining individual records for tracking purposes
Immediately assign an outcome type of euthanasia to simplify the record
Delete the record entirely until an owner arrives to verify details
e: Unknown history must be explicitly documented as 'unknown' in the relevant fields. Leaving fields blank implies the information was not collected (a compliance failure). Documenting 'unknown' accurately reflects what is known and maintains a compliant individual record.

q: A dog's record shows: Intake Kennel 1A, June 1 to June 3; Foster Home B, June 4 to June 10; Adoption Ward Run 5, June 11 onward. This detailed entry fulfills which tracking mandate?
o: Fundamental intake description metrics
Housing locations tracked by time under in-shelter care activities
Outcome type and date metadata matching
Phase B microchip triad scanning protocol
e: This is a compliant housing location by time entry, one of the three in-shelter care activity tracking requirements. It allows the shelter to reconstruct exactly where the animal was at any point during its stay, which is essential for outbreak contact tracing.

q: A data analyst needs historical information about the types of environments and cohabitants animals lived with before entering the shelter. Which record section should they review?
o: In-shelter care activities and medical procedures log
History: people and animals lived with, and home environment
Fundamental intake weight and body condition scores
Outcome type and outcome date records
e: Previous cohabitants (people and animals lived with) and home environment are two of the five Phase C history items. They are collected at intake from the surrendering owner or transfer paperwork and are not updated during the shelter stay.

q: An intake team scans a dog and records a positive microchip number in the file, then documents a distinctive white spot on the dog's left shoulder. These entries satisfy which record component?
o: In-shelter behavioral plans
Microchip scan results and identifying markings (the ID triad, Phase B)
Fundamental intake age category and sex data (Phase A)
Outcome type and date metadata
e: Microchip scan results (the specific chip number found on scanning) and identifying markings (the white shoulder spot) are two of the three components of the identification triad. Together with the intake photograph, they form Phase B of the record.

q: A shelter database shows an entry: 'ID: Cat #992, Intake Type: Owner Surrender, Date: Jan 20, Species: Feline, Age: 3 Years, Sex: Female, Status: Spayed, Description: Calico.' Which of the nine Phase A items is missing?
o: Date of intake
Spay-neuter status
Weight or BCS
Unique identifier
e: The entry contains 8 of the 9 mandatory items: unique ID, intake type, date, species, age, sex, spay-neuter status, and physical description. The missing item is weight or Body Condition Score (BCS), item 9 of 9.

q: A dog displayed high levels of fear and avoidance during novel stimulus exposure on day 2 of its stay. Where does this behavioral observation belong in the record?
o: Phase C historical background context from previous owners
In-shelter care activities: behavioral findings, plans, and treatments
Phase A fundamental intake description
Identifying markings and microchip triad results
e: Behavioral observations made during the shelter stay are documented under in-shelter care activities, specifically under behavioral findings, plans, and treatments. This is distinct from the animal's pre-shelter behavioral history, which is documented in Phase C.

q: Why must a unique identifier be assigned at or prior to admission rather than after a few days of intake processing?
o: To lock the animal's live outcome potential score into the system
To ensure consistency and accuracy in care and record-keeping from the absolute start of the animal's stay
To bypass the requirement for housing location tracking
To eliminate the need for rabies vaccination history documentation
e: ID assignment at or before admission guarantees that every clinical action, housing move, and behavioral observation during the animal's entire stay is reliably linked to the correct individual. Delays create a window where care cannot be accurately attributed.

q: A dog is reclaimed by its owner on March 5. The owner pays the fee and leaves with the dog. Which fields must be completed to officially close this shelter stay?
o: In-shelter medical findings and housing locations by time
Outcome type (Return to Owner) and the exact date March 5
Historical vaccination data and previous home environment records
Fundamental intake weight and body condition score
e: Closing a shelter stay record requires two outcome fields: the specific outcome type (Return to Owner) and the exact date of that outcome (March 5). Together, these entries close the file and feed into ALOS and live release rate calculations.

q: An auditor finds that for multiple owner surrenders, the 'medical conditions and services received' history field was left blank even though owners provided this information at surrender. What type of non-compliance has occurred?
o: Failure to record in-shelter care activities
Failure to fully populate the mandatory history items with available information
Violation of the Phase B microchip scanning triad requirement
Omission of fundamental outcome metadata fields
e: History items must be populated with available information provided by the owner. Leaving a field blank when the information was available (not genuinely unknown) is non-compliance with the history documentation requirement, specifically the medical conditions and services received sub-item.

q: A shelter adopts a policy to stop requiring intake photographs to save digital storage space. Why does this policy violate record-keeping standards?
o: A photograph is an explicitly mandated component of the identification dataset for every individual record
Photographs are the only mechanism for calculating daily body condition scores
Removing photographs automatically deletes the rabies vaccination history
Individual files are completely illegal without photographs
e: The photograph is one of the three mandatory components of the Phase B identification triad. It is not optional. A policy that eliminates photographs fails to meet the mandatory identification standard regardless of storage cost justifications.

q: A stray dog undergoes emergency orthopedic surgery. Where must the pre-surgical findings, procedure, anesthetic protocol, and post-operative medications be documented?
o: In the Phase C history log under past medical conditions
In-shelter care activities: medical findings, treatments, and procedures
In the Phase A fundamental intake age and sex metadata fields
In the final outcome type and date parameters
e: All clinical actions performed during the shelter stay, including emergency surgeries, are documented under in-shelter care activities: medical findings, treatments, and procedures. Pre-shelter medical history (Phase C) covers what happened before admission, not during.

q: An intake clerk enters 'Adult' for age/age category for a rabbit. Which component of the core dataset does this entry fulfill?
o: One of the five Phase C historical context items
One of the nine Phase A mandatory fundamental intake items
The in-shelter care behavioral plan
The Phase B identification triad framework
e: Age or age category is item 5 of the nine mandatory Phase A fundamental intake items. 'Adult' is an appropriate age category entry. For SAC reporting purposes, the relevant cutoff is under 5 months (pediatric) versus 5 months and older (adult).

q: A dog transferred from an out-of-state shelter arrives with extensive documentation of its pre-shelter behavioral history. In which record section must this information be preserved?
o: Outcome type metadata fields
Phase C history
In-shelter care location logs
Phase A fundamental intake physical descriptions
e: Historical behavioral information documented before the animal entered this shelter belongs in Phase C history, specifically under behavioral events and experiences. Transfer paperwork from another organization is treated the same as an owner-provided history.

q: A shelter manager wants to calculate how many times animals are moved between housing areas during their stay, to assess operational stress. Which record metric provides this timeline?
o: Unique identifier and intake type
Housing locations by time, recorded under in-shelter care activities
Intake photographs paired with microchip scan results
Outcome type combined with the date of outcome
e: Housing locations by time is the only metric that records each move between areas with associated dates. Analyzing the frequency and pattern of housing moves from this field allows managers to assess operational disruption and its welfare impact on residents.

q: A shelter uses a 125 kHz legacy scanner for all intake microchip scans. A stray dog reads as 'no chip detected.' The dog is later claimed by its owner who provides documentation of a 134.2 kHz ISO microchip implanted last year. What went wrong?
o: The chip deactivated during impoundment stress
The shelter's legacy scanner cannot read ISO 134.2 kHz chips, producing a false negative
ISO chips are undetectable for the first 24 hours after a stressful event
The chip migrated to the tail and requires ultrasound localization
e: ISO microchips operate at 134.2 kHz. A 125 kHz legacy scanner cannot detect this frequency and returns a false negative. Universal (ISO-compatible) scanners reading both 125 kHz and 134.2 kHz are required in all shelters to prevent this failure.

q: An intake technician performs one forward pass over a stray cat with a universal scanner, gets no reading, and records 'no chip.' Why is this documentation non-compliant?
o: One forward pass is the required protocol; backward passes are optional
At minimum two passes (forward and backward) are required before documenting 'no chip detected,' since chips frequently migrate from the interscapular implant site
Only credentialed staff may perform microchip scans, making any technician scan non-compliant
The scan must occur in a shielded room before the result can be documented
e: Chips commonly migrate from the standard interscapular implant site to the neck, flank, or limbs. A single-direction pass may miss a migrated chip. At minimum two passes in opposite directions are required before documenting 'no chip detected.'

q: After scanning a stray dog twice and reading a 15-digit number, the number returns no matches across three microchip registries. What is the correct documentation?
o: Record 'no chip' since the number is unregistered and therefore useless
Record the exact 15-digit chip number and note that it returned no match in the specific registries searched
Delete the entry and flag the dog as unidentified
Contact the DEA to report an unregistered implant
e: The chip number must be recorded exactly as read even if no registry match is found. No single registry is comprehensive. The owner may recognize the number, and documenting the registries searched creates a defensible intake record supporting owner reclaim.

q: During an intake shift, a dog is moved from Run 3 to Run 7 for cleaning but the cage card is left on Run 3. A second worker later medicates the new occupant of Run 3 using the card's instructions. What ID failure occurred?
o: ISO chip frequency mismatch between the two dogs
Cage card identity mismatch — the card remained with the enclosure instead of traveling with the animal, causing medication to reach the wrong individual
Phase C history was not transferred between kennel runs
Phase A intake type was not updated to reflect the housing move
e: Cage cards identify the enclosure, not the animal. When an animal moves without its card, the card associates with the new occupant — a potentially dangerous error. Cage cards must travel with the animal through every housing move, with simultaneous digital housing location update.

q: A dog's ISO microchip number begins with '985.' What does this prefix signify?
o: The dog was chipped with a 125 kHz legacy North American chip
'985' is a common ISO 11784 country-manufacturer prefix for chips implanted in the United States; the 15-digit format confirms this is an ISO-standard chip
The chip was implanted before 2005 and may be unreadable on modern scanners
It indicates a canine-specific encoding distinct from feline chips
e: The ISO 15-digit format includes a 3-digit country or manufacturer prefix. '985' and '900' are common prefixes for ISO chips implanted in the US. A 15-digit number beginning with 985 indicates an ISO 11784/11785-compliant chip requiring a universal 134.2 kHz-capable scanner.
